name: W. Morton Fullerton
bio: American journalist, Paris correspondent of The Times. In June 1899 Wilde, quite without money, asked him for a loan of 100 francs, to be sent to 'Monsieur Sebastian Melmoth'. Fullerton replied that he was distressed to have left the appeal unanswered so long, and addressed him by the alias without comment.
bio_note: What is not asserted: Fullerton's own documented relationships with men, and his later affair with Edith Wharton, are outside this volume; this node does not borrow them. The third letter, at printed 1155, is located and unread. Dates not recorded and none inferred.

sources.quote: My dear Fullerton, I find myself in very great trouble owing to not getting some money I expected, from America, where it is owing to me. Would it be an inconvenience to you to lend me 100 francs? I receive my quarterly allowance, such as it is, on July 1st, when I will be able to return it to you. At present I am quite without money, and I hope you will not mind my asking you this favour. If you are able to do this would you send it to me, Monsieur Sebastian Melmoth, at the above address? Believe me, truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to W. Morton Fullerton, [June 1899], Hotel Marsollier (MS Harvard) - quoted whole. 'Sebastian Melmoth' is italicised in the printed text: the money has to be addressed to the alias, which is the exile's whole condition in one clause. Eighteen months before his death.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde asking a journalist for a hundred francs, under his assumed name.
sources.provenance: PDF page 1200; printed folio 1154 confirmed on the rendered page image.

sources.quote: My dear Melmoth, I am distressed to have left your touching appeal unanswered for so long. But I have been on conge in the patrie of Stendhal, and had cognisance of your gene only yesterday.
sources.context: Fullerton's reply, 3 June 1899, 35 boulevard des Capucines (MS Clark), quoted by the editors. His own words, which few people on this map get. He addresses Wilde by the alias without remark - 'My dear Melmoth' - which is what the courtesy of that circle looked like in practice. 'conge' is leave; 'gene' is embarrassment or want.
sources.speaker: W. Morton Fullerton
sources.supports: That the appeal was answered, and how Fullerton addressed him.
